title: IP addresses
hook: For your request to reach the right server out of billions, every device needs its own address.

steps.caption: Your request is addressed to a specific IP — a number, not a name.

nodeCaptions.client: Your device has its own address on the local network — that's the 192.168.x.x number.
nodeCaptions.router: The router looks at the destination address and forwards the packet toward it.

steps.caption: The router hands it off, hop by hop, until it reaches the address it's looking for.

nodeCaptions.server: This server's IP address is fixed and public — it's how the whole internet finds it.

takeaways: An IP address is a number, like a street address, not a name — that's what makes it routable.
Your device's local address (192.168.x.x) and a public server's address are both IPs, just on different networks.
Every hop between you and a server forwards your packet based on nothing but that destination number.

quiz.question: Why does a packet need a destination IP address instead of just a name like "the server"?
choices: Names take up more storage than numbers
Routers forward packets based on a numeric address they can look up quickly, not on human-readable names
IP addresses are more secure than names
It's a legacy requirement with no real reason today
quiz.explanation: Routing hardware is built to match and forward numeric addresses fast — names are a convenience layer on top, which is exactly what DNS provides.
